preamble: Voicing of [s] to [z] is one of the most common consonant changes. It occurs between vowels or other voiced sounds, as in Western Romance and Old English; after an unaccented vowel, under Proto-Germanic Verner's law; and before voiced obstruents through regressive assimilation, as in Russian. In many languages it is allophonic; in others it became phonemic once the conditioning was lost.

examples.note: Intervocalic voicing of single /s/ in Western Romance.
Stages as given by Wikipedia (Proto-Germanic language); both *s follow unaccented vowels.

languageExamples.context: Between voiced sounds after a stressed syllable

examples.note: The fricatives /f θ s/ had voiced allophones [v ð z] between voiced sounds after a stressed syllable; s spelled both [s] and [z].

languageExamples.context: Before a voiced obstruent (regressive voicing assimilation)

examples.note: Regressive voicing assimilation: a voiceless obstruent becomes voiced before a voiced obstruent.

All fricatives became voiced in non-final syllables; Copala (skaʔ) and Itunyoso (sikaʔ) keep s. In final syllables fricatives are usually voiced in both Chicahuaxtla and Copala, as in *rasũũ 'thing' > razũ, Copala razũũ.
